passage: Akash, twenty, typed forms all day at a small computer shop near the tehsil office, hunched over a monitor that sat too low on a wooden table. By evening his neck burned and his lower back felt like a knot. His sister Indu watched him groan as he sat down to dinner. "You sit like a question mark," she said. The next morning he raised the monitor on two bricks from the yard and pushed a folded towel behind his back. Every hour, when the temple loudspeaker crackled, he stood and stretched his arms. He started walking to the canal and back after closing, and swapped his daily packet of chips for Amma's roasted chana. A month later his neck felt looser. "If it comes back," Indu said, "see the doctor."

qa.q: What did Akash use to raise his monitor?
qa.a: Two bricks from the yard.

qa.q: Why might Akash have groaned as he sat down to dinner?
qa.a: His neck and back were aching from hunching over the low monitor all day, and he was tired and uncomfortable.

qa.q: Which change made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Raising the monitor, because it fixed the posture that was causing his pain, while the stretching and walking helped build the habit.

qa.q: How does Indu see her brother's health?
qa.a: She notices his pain and cares enough to tease him into changing, and she wants him to see a doctor if it returns.

grounding: Shows a young man in a small town building ergonomic habits, activity and better eating into daily life.

passage: Ada, twenty-two, had been interning at a design firm in Osaka for three months when her right wrist began to ache every evening. She had been working on her laptop from the sofa of her tiny flat after hours, and eating convenience-store noodles at her desk. Her colleague Aiko noticed her rubbing her wrist during a meeting. "Is your chair even set up?" Aiko asked afterwards, and showed her how to lower the seat so her elbows rested at the desk's height. She lent Ada an old keyboard. Ada began taking a fifteen-minute walk by the river at lunch, carrying a bento she packed the night before. She stopped working from the sofa. After a few weeks the ache faded. She told Aiko, "I didn't know bodies needed setting up too."

qa.q: Where did Ada start walking at lunch?
qa.a: By the river.

qa.q: What does Ada's remark about bodies needing setting up suggest?
qa.a: She has realised her body is affected by her habits, and she seems relieved and a bit surprised that small changes helped.

qa.q: How could the firm help interns like Ada from the start?
qa.a: It could show new staff how to set up chairs and screens properly and encourage real lunch breaks.

qa.q: What is it like for Aiko to notice Ada rubbing her wrist?
qa.a: She seems concerned and takes practical steps to help, perhaps having learned these lessons herself.

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad adopting ergonomic, active and healthier routines at work.

passage: The college athletics club track was still damp at six in the morning. Kalyani, nineteen, had signed up for the half-marathon and was trying to run the full distance on day one. By the second week her shins throbbed and she was sleeping badly. Coach Varun called her over. "You're running like you have one week to live," he said. "Build it slowly. Three run days, rest days between. Sleep. Eat proper meals, not just biscuits between lectures." He showed her calf stretches against the fence. Kalyani grumbled but made a chart on her hostel wall: runs, stretches, sleep time. She started carrying a steel bottle of water and a banana to class. By the end of the term, she ran further than ever, and her shins didn't complain.

qa.q: What did Kalyani carry to class?
qa.a: A steel bottle of water and a banana.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani grumble at the coach's advice?
qa.a: She was eager to see fast results and probably felt frustrated at being told to slow down.

qa.q: Why did the coach's plan work better than her first approach?
qa.a: Building up gradually with rest, sleep and proper food let her body adapt instead of breaking down.

qa.q: How might Varun feel at the end of the term?
qa.a: He would likely feel satisfied to see her running further without pain, since she listened to his advice.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a college sports club learning long-term endurance habits, rest and nutrition.

passage:
Dear Pranav,
You were right about my laptop, and I hate that you were right. Three months into the job I was hunched on my bed working, eating lunch over the keyboard, and by evening my neck felt like wood. I kept thinking, I'm twenty-two, this can't be happening. So I copied your setup. Laptop on a stack of old textbooks so the screen sits at eye level, a cheap separate keyboard, a proper chair from the second-hand market. I set reminders to stand and stretch through the day, and I walk to the vegetable market instead of ordering in. I've started cooking dal and sabzi on Sundays for the week so I'm not living on chips. My neck is better. When it wasn't improving at first, I did get it checked, like you nagged me to. Thank you for nagging.
Sabina

qa.q: What did Sabina use to raise the laptop?
qa.a: A stack of old textbooks.

qa.q: What does 'I hate that you were right' reveal about Sabina's feelings?
qa.a: Sabina is a bit embarrassed to admit ignoring Pranav's advice, but grateful and relieved it worked.

qa.q: What made Sabina's changes likely to last?
qa.a: They were simple and cheap and built into Sabina's routine, like cooking on Sundays and walking to the market.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel reading 'Thank you for nagging'?
qa.a: Amused and glad that the nagging helped a friend. 😊

grounding: Shows a young adult setting up a better desk, moving more and cooking regularly as lasting self-care habits.

passage: 'Shreya, you keep asking why I'm up at six now. Okay. In first year I got breathless climbing to the fourth-floor lab. Four floors! I'm twenty. That scared me a little. So I joined the college running group, the slow one. The first week I walked more than I ran and felt so embarrassed. But nobody cared. The captain just said, "Simran, show up, that's the whole trick." So I did. I started carrying a proper tiffin, rice and vegetables and curd, instead of skipping breakfast and eating chips at eleven. Last week I climbed to the lab talking the whole way and didn't notice till I got there. It's not about looks. It's that my body feels like it's on my side now.'

qa.q: Which floor was the lab on?
qa.a: The fourth floor.

qa.q: Why did Simran feel embarrassed in the first week?
qa.a: Simran walked more than ran and worried about being judged by the others.

qa.q: Which advice from the captain could help other beginners?
qa.a: 'Show up, that's the whole trick', because at the start regular effort matters more than speed.

qa.q: How might Shreya see Simran's change?
qa.a: Shreya is curious about the early mornings and may be inspired to join too.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult building stamina and better eating habits through a steady routine.
